=== session.md
     1	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
     2	
     3	The main session and all its agents run their commands on one machine, the session's machine. An agent is another Claude that works for the session: an Agent-tool worker or a Workflow agent.
     4	
     5	## The Bash tool
     6	
     7	- Every Bash call starts a new shell. Variables and shell functions that one call defines are gone in the next call. In an agent, the working directory is also reset. So set up each call again (`build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call").
     8	- The Bash tool's timeout is 2 minutes by default and 10 minutes at most. If a call reaches the timeout, the tool cuts it off: it kills the command, or it moves the command to the background, where you must find it again.
     9	
    10	## Long commands
    11	
    12	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it in the background with a log, and poll the log. Do not pipe a long command through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing. Grep the log instead. Put the log under your tree's `tmp/`.
    13	
    14	Define the two functions in each call that uses them:
    15	
    16	    run_bg () {      # run_bg <logfile> "<command>"
    17	        nohup bash -c "( $2 ) > '$1' 2>&1; echo EXIT=\$? >> '$1'" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
    18	    }
    19	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
    20	        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
    21	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
    22	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
    23	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
    24	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
    25	        done
    26	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
    27	    }
    28	
    29	- `run_bg` starts the command detached. It writes the command's output to the log, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`.
    30	- `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0. If not, it returns 1: call it again, in a new call.
    31	
    32	## Waits and the prompt cache
    33	
    34	The prompt cache is the API's copy of a conversation's context. For an agent, it lives five minutes. For the main session, it lives one hour. A call inside that time reads the cache and renews it. The first call after a longer wait writes the whole context again. Late in a long task, that is hundreds of thousands of tokens.
    35	
    36	- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s. Do not chain sleeps in one call past that.
    37	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
    38	
    39	## Sharing the machine
    40	
    41	All agents of the session share the machine's cores. If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. The machine's figures are in the `cloud-container` skill.
    42	
    43	## Stopping processes
    44	
    45	Your tree is the worktree or directory that your work runs in. Stop or kill only the processes that run under its path.
    46	
    47	- To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
    48	- Kill by process id. Do not kill by a script's name across the machine: other agents run copies of the same scripts.
    49	- Do not use `pkill -f <pattern>`. If the pattern is in your own call's command line, it also matches the shell of that call, and it kills your call.
    50	
    51	## Interrupts and stops of the process
    52	
    53	- An interrupt is a stop of the session's turn (the stop button). It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, Workflow agents and Agent-tool workers alike. A message sent while the session is busy kills nothing.
    54	- A stop of the session's process kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the disk (worktrees, uncommitted edits, logs) and the transcripts. A command started with `nohup`, as `run_bg` starts it, survives a stop of the process. On the cloud platform, it does not survive a restart of the VM (the `cloud-container` skill).
    55	
    56	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop:
    57	
    58	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
    59	2. If a log ends with its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete, that step is done. Do not run it again, unless the tree changed after the log was written.
    60	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it. Do not start a second one.
    61	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
    62	
    63	## The automatic permission check
    64	
    65	In auto mode, an automatic check approves each step, not the curator. The check refuses some steps, also after the curator approved them in chat. In manual mode, every command of every agent waits for the curator's approval.
    66	
    67	If the check refuses a step:
    68	
    69	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
    70	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through belongs to the curator: a switch of the session to manual approval, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
=== toolchain.md
     1	# Toolchain and generated sources
     2	
     3	Read this part if the build fails or behaves oddly, before you change the JDK or the build file, and before you edit anything generated.
     4	
     5	- scalac runs through `scala.tools.nsc.Main`, because Scala 2.13 has no ant tasks.
     6	- ASM is vendored in `ProjectFortress/third_party/asm/`. In that package, Fortress's own `asmbytecodeoptimizer.Opcodes` hides `org.objectweb.asm.Opcodes`.
     7	- All sources compile as UTF-8.
     8	- Every javac task sets `target=` to the source version. The reason: ASM 3.1 reads the class of every `import java`, and it cannot read newer classfiles.
     9	- Fortress writes its classfiles at version 1.6, because the rewriting at load time keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise this version.
    10	- In a fresh container, run `apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant`. `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` does the whole setup of a fresh container: the packages (LaTeX for the specification among them), the build, and the transcript backup. The transcript backup is the hook that copies every session's transcripts to an orphan branch and pushes it (the `cloud-container` skill).
    11	- JDK 25 is the current JDK (`JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`). JDK 21 is installed beside it. JDKs 8, 11, 17 and 21 also build the tree and pass the gate. Versions and the classfile level: `explorations/modernization-plan.md`.
    12	- The generated sources are committed. `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` generates `nodes/` (over 1,000 files), `scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala` and `Library/FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi`. The Rats! grammars generate the parsers. Edit the input, never the output.
    13	- If a build changes generated sources, investigate it as a regression. Do not revert it as noise.
    14	- If scalac reports arity errors in `S*Pattern` nodes, the generated nodes are stale. Run `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast && ant compileAll`.
=== worktrees.md
     1	# The base, worktrees seeded from its build, and the old code beside the new
     2	
     3	Read this part if you need a worktree of your own, or the behaviour of the code before your edit.
     4	
     5	## The base and the base build
     6	
     7	The base is the commit that your work starts from: the commit under your first change. Your brief may name it.
     8	
     9	The base build is a clean worktree at the base, built once in place by ant. Every other worktree of the work is seeded from it, and the old code runs from it. After it is built, do not compile, build or run anything in it, except through `old-fortress.sh` (below).
    10	
    11	- If your brief names a base build, use it. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`.
    12	- If not, `git worktree list` shows the worktrees on the machine. A worktree can be your base build if `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base, `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing, and it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
    13	- If no worktree qualifies, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s. Say so in your report.
    14	
    15	      git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
    16	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
    17	      ant compileAll
    18	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
    19	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
    20	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
    21	
    22	If you check another agent's fix against its old code, the base build's commit must be the commit that the fix starts from. Read the base build's commit with `git -C <base-build> rev-parse HEAD`. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. Otherwise, it starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`. Old code from another commit measures another tree.
    23	
    24	## Worktrees seeded from the base build
    25	
    26	Seed a worktree instead of building it. Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path at once, with the library already compiled:
    27	
    28	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
    29	
    30	- `<branch>` is a local branch, or else origin's branch, or else a new branch cut from `<start-point>` (default: the base's commit). With `-`, the script makes a detached worktree.
    31	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
    32	- If the worktree already has a build, the script leaves it, so a relaunch keeps its own build. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces the build.
    33	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base. Recompile them (`build-and-caches.md`) before a compiled run.
    34	- If `ProjectFortress/src` differs from the base, the script warns: the copied build is the base's. Run `ant compileAll`, which recompiles exactly the files that differ. Then run the library order.
    35	- The base build's file dates must be a build's dates. So the base build must be built in place by ant, or seeded by this script.
    36	
    37	Do not symlink or plainly copy another tree's build or caches. Cache entries are keyed by absolute path, and with a symlinked build every cache path resolves to the other tree. The script translates the paths.
    38	
    39	Two agents must never compile into one cache, because every compile rewrites cache files of the tree that it runs in. Your brief says where you work. If you need a build of your own, seed a worktree of your own and work only there.
    40	
    41	Put scratch under `<worktree>/tmp/`, which is gitignored. Set up each call as `build-and-caches.md` says, and check that `echo $FORTRESS_HOME` prints your worktree.
    42	
    43	Two lines of the untracked `.git/info/exclude` keep the main tree's `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` out of `git status`. A fresh clone lacks these lines, so these paths show as untracked there. Never commit them.
    44	
    45	## The old code beside the new
    46	
    47	You may need the base's behaviour after your worktree holds an edit: to see a test fail, or to compare a program's old and new output. Do not revert and rebuild your worktree for this. Run the base build through `old-fortress.sh`, with a private caches folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
    48	
    49	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    50	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    51	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    52	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    53	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test   # a compiled .test
    54

    37	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
    38

    45	### Keeping the caches through a build
    46

    68	## The caches
    69	
    70	An api is a component's interface. The component's `.fsi` file declares it, and the component's `.fss` file implements it.
    71	
    72	The caches are in `default_repository/caches/`. All of them are gitignored.
    73	
    74	- `analyzed_cache/`, `*parsed_cache/`: the front end's analysis. The name of each entry is a hash of its source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path.
    75	- `interpreter_cache/`, `environment_cache/`: walk's caches.
    76	- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component. The library's jars have api-qualified names, for example `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
    77	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for `import java` natives.
    78	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one (`linker/RepoState.java:366-385`), also in a private caches folder.
    79	
    80	Fortress uses an entry if the entry is not older than its source. A changed api makes every entry that imports it stale. Entries are keyed by absolute path, so a plain copy of another tree's caches does not work. Seed a tree instead (`worktrees.md`).
    81	
    82	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the ladder driver and both ant suites. A private caches folder outside `tmp/` is not gitignored.
    83	
    84	## After an edit, what to rebuild
    85	
    86	Walk reads an edited Fortress source again on its next run. The compiled path sees an edit only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it. If you skip the step for your edit:
    87	
    88	- after an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning;
    89	- after an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError`.
    90	
    91	The compiled path builds five library components, in the library order (below). They are `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type `Any`, which both libraries share, and the compiler's own `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin`, `Library/CompilerLibrary`, `Library/CompilerAlgebra` and `Library/CompilerSystem`.
    92	
    93	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. CompilerBuiltin takes about 60 s, CompilerLibrary about 25 s, the others 2 to 16 s. Programs need no recompile.
    94	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order, about 100 s. Every api depends on these four.
    95	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
    96	- If you edited another file of the interpreter's library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and the others): do nothing. Walk reads the file again on its next run, compiled programs do not link it yet, and the checker measurements read it from source.
    97	- If you edited Java or Scala: run `ant compileAll`, then the library order before the next compiled run. After some edits you can keep the caches (above).
    98	
    99	If you see old behaviour or a `NoSuchMethodError` after an edit, you skipped a step above. Do that step now. Do not delete the caches to fix it: that works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. Only `ant compileAll` deletes the caches. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
   100	
   101	The library order takes about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll` (AnyType 17 s, CompilerBuiltin 63 s, CompilerLibrary 27 s, CompilerAlgebra 2 s, CompilerSystem 2 s):
   102	
   103	    cd ProjectFortress
   104	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
   105	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss
   106	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss
   107	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss
   108	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss
   109	
   110	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`.    111	
   112	Symptoms:
   113

     1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run-time
     2	
     3	The code is under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`:
     4	
     5	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
     6	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, `phases/PhaseOrder.java`, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
     7	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
     8	- `compiler/runtimeValues/` and `nativeHelpers/`.
     9	
    10	The compiler does not compile every construct yet. For some constructs, the code generator calls `sayWhat`, which throws a `CompilerError`. This is called a `sayWhat` wall.
    11	
    12	## Running
    13	
    14	    cd ProjectFortress
    15	    # after any ant compileAll: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    16	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    17	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
    18	
    19	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s. The compile of a program never builds the library components that it imports (`System`, `CompilerSystem`). The library order builds them.
    20	
    21	The phases are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN. The syntax tree is the only intermediate form. A switch of `Shell.java`, set for each command, decides which desugarings run; the phase list does not. The checker runs only on this path.
    22	
    23	Before you edit, find where the fix belongs:
    24	
    25	- `explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md` gives each feature's parser rule, checker class, interpreter site, code-generator site and prelude location.
    26	- `explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md` gives both pipelines, phase by phase.
    27	
    28	## The `fortress` commands
    29	
    30	`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java` (`:403-487`) dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
    31	
    32	- Regular use: walk (`bin/fortress P.fss`, the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`), `compile`, `run`, and `junit X.test` for one compiled test by hand (`tests-running.md`).
    33	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`. `typecheck` checks against the compiler's own prelude, so it says nothing about an interpreter program.
    34	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
    35	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
    36	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java:371-386`). Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches. The compiler's call sets the `extends Object` bound before disambiguation; walk's call does not.
    37	
    38	## What the code generator does
    39	
    40	- It makes every Fortress type a JVM reference type. For example, `RR64` becomes the run-time class `FRR64`. It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
    41	- It gives each overloaded name one dispatch method. The method tests the argument types from the most specific declaration to the least specific.
    42	- It compiles a generic declaration once, as a template. At the first load of each instantiation (`Box⟦RR64⟧`), `InstantiatingClassloader` makes the instantiation by rewriting the template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6: do not raise it.
    43	- A size static argument is passed at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`.
    44	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
    45	
    46	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
    47	
    48	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. It also builds `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss`, the top type that both libraries share, and `Library/CompilerSystem.fss`, the compiled path's `System`.
    49	
    50	- Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files. The interpreter's library becomes the library that the compiler checks, and the three files are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay (`library.md`).
    51	- The record does not yet say what happens to `CompilerSystem` at the switch-over.
    52	
    53	Natives: write `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in the `.fss` file. It binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
    54	
    55	- The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
    56	- After you change a helper's signature, run the plain `ant compileAll` (`build-and-caches.md`). It deletes the caches, and with them the helper's stale wrapper in `nativewrapper_cache/`. If you keep the caches, the run links the old signature.
    57	
    58	## Testing an edit here
    59	
    60	- After a Java or Scala edit, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order before any compiled run.
    61	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or of the code generator, compile the edited class against the build's class path into a scratch directory. Put that directory first on the class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh` is a working example: it runs `javac` against `bin/fortress_classpath` and puts the output ahead of `ProjectFortress/build`.
    62	- Give such a run its own caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES` under your `tmp/`), because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
    63	- After a checker edit, run your own tests through `junit.sh`. You may run the compiler and library tracks whole, once, on your final code (`tests-running.md`).
    64	- After a code-generator edit, run your own tests through `junit.sh`. The record names no whole track for this edit: leave the whole tracks to the gate (`tests-running.md`).
    65	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`). Also run your own checks at `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `4`.
    66	- For the `XXX` shapes of a code-generator wall, a refusal at compile time or a crash at run time, read `tests-writing.md`.
    67	
    68	## Known shapes
    69	
    70	- The compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object` before disambiguation. This rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type. The specification and the measurements use the bound `Any`. The difference stays until the switch-over.
    71	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
    72	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A failed library compile writes nothing, or only its jar.
    73	- `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude, not the interpreter's prelude.

     1	# The interpreter (walk)
     2	
     3	The code is in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/`: `evaluator/` (the tree walker), `glue/` (the natives), `env/` and `rewrite/`. The library is `Library/` with `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`. The tests are in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, and `testSystem` runs them.
     4	
     5	## Running a program
     6	
     7	    bin/fortress P.fss              # the same as: bin/fortress walk P.fss
     8	
     9	- The file name without `.fss` must be the component's name. Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
    10	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
    11	- `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets the size of the work-stealing pool. Your setup sets 1. If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs. A `for` loop is parallel unless every generator is `seq`. Walk evaluates the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator in parallel.
    12	- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches. After you edit a library source, walk reads it again on its next run: rebuild nothing and delete nothing.
    13	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/mandelbrot_canonical.fss`, which prints its picture, or `bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, which prints nothing and exits 0. Do not use `explorations/claude_demo.fss` for this: it dies under walk at its `SUM` with no static argument written, a known defect (ledger row 424). `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.
    14	
    15	## The model program
    16	
    17	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]` runs its two checks at once: `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplCheck.fss`. Each check starts from an empty private cache and has a 90-minute timeout.
    18	
    19	- In auto mode (`session.md`), the automatic permission check refuses the script's `rm -rf` of its own work directories. If the check refuses it, do not run the checks another way. Report that they did not run (`session.md`, "The automatic permission check").
    20	- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.
    21	
    22	## What walk does not do
    23	
    24	- Walk does no static checking. Its type-checking phase does nothing, and no switch turns it on. So every "type error" that walk prints is a dispatch failure at run time, and walk accepts programs that the specification forbids.
    25	- `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude, so it says nothing about an interpreter program.
    26	- Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. This is an accepted limit until the switch-over.
    27	- Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Never compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
    28	- Walk's speed does not matter. Do not take or record a timing of the interpreter, and do not edit anything for speed.
    29	- `import java` is how the compiled path binds natives. Under walk, it is wired but unfinished, and no test uses it. Walk's natives are the `builtinPrimitive` strings (below).
    30	
    31	## Natives
    32	
    33	The library binds walk's natives by `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")` strings in its `.fss` files. The classes are under `interpreter/glue/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them.
    34	
    35	A native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees. `Int.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java` does it like this:
    36	
    37	    throw new FortressError((FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(name));
    38	
    39	Every other Java exception that a native throws is mapped as before. Division by zero still ends the run.
    40	
    41	## Checks at load
    42	
    43	At load, walk checks the `comprises` clauses of the program's main component. It refuses a program with an extender that a clause does not allow. It does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. To test such a refusal, name it with `load_exception_contains` in a `Name.test` file beside the program (`tests-writing.md`).
    44	
    45	## After an edit here
    46	
    47	- After you edit Java under `interpreter/`, run `ant compileAll` (`build-and-caches.md`). Run the library order only before a compiled run.
    48	- The suite that your edit reaches is `testSystem`. Run your own tests through `harness-one.sh`. You may run the whole `testSystem` once, on your final code. Quote its verdict (`tests-running.md`).
    49	- Walk shares the parser and the early phases with the compiler. So an edit to the desugarers, the disambiguator or the switches of `Shell.java` can change both paths.
=== library.md
     1	# The library
     2	
     3	The one library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
     4	
     5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it.
     6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
     7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. The compiled path builds it in the library order, so an edit to it needs that step (`build-and-caches.md`).
     8	
     9	Walk runs this library today. At the switch-over, the compiled checker accepts it and the compiler compiles it, and the compiler's own prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`) is deleted. Until then:
    10	
    11	- Do not add a declaration to the compiler's prelude. Put extensions into this library itself, never into a tree of our own.
    12	
    13	## Designing a change
    14	
    15	- Before you design a change, study the existing parts of the library for the same family of declarations. Use their patterns to extend the library in its own way.
    16	- Do not design a fix from a reading of the specification alone, or from a workaround on the user's side.
    17	- If a rule of the language or of the checker refuses the way you want to write something, find how the library already writes that kind of thing, and do the same.
    18	- Before you choose, search the decisions on record (`records.md`).
    19	- The specification says what the language means (`specification.md`). If the library's practice and the specification's text disagree, and no decision on record settles it, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
    20	
    21	These points are decisions on record. Do not reopen them:
    22	
    23	- Exclusion (`excludes`, `comprises`) is used all over the library. The compiled checker keeps the multiple-instantiation exclusion rule.
    24	- The numeric tower is flat. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` are siblings under `Number`, and each carries its own algebra. A wider type has a `coerce` from each narrower type. Walk converts by coercion at dispatch.
    25	- The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`.
    26	- A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.
    27	- A conversion is applied to make a call possible. It never changes which declaration runs if one already fits.
    28	
    29	## Editing
    30	
    31	- After an edit, walk reads the file again on its next run: rebuild nothing. The compiled path does not link this library yet.
    32	- A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span, and of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Compare parse trees or diagnostics only after you map the positions back (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/parse-compare.sh` and `remap-lines.py`).
    33	- `Library/FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. Never edit them by hand.
    34	- Natives are `builtinPrimitive("...")` strings that name classes under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`).
    35	- If a library change breaks a line of a team test, respell the line and keep the value that it checks. Never delete it. List it in your report with its before and after.
    36	
    37	A note for the switch-over, not a step of a change today: the compiled path will need a static helper in `nativeHelpers/` for each native. Every program's output goes through the native `Writer`, because `println` writes through `stdOut`. So the first compiled program on this library needs `Writer`'s natives. PLAN item 35 decides the form of the binding.
    38	
    39	Put tests of walk's behaviour of the library in `ProjectFortress/tests/`. `library_tests/` holds compiled tests of the compiler's prelude.
=== specification.md
     1	# The specification
     2	
     3	- `Specification/` is the team's working draft, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a later source of the team's says otherwise (below).
     4	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy, called "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Never edit this copy.
     5	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
     6	
     7	## Weighing the sources
     8	
     9	The aim is to finish what the designers intended, not to redesign. The team learned as it built, so if two of its sources conflict, the later one outweighs the earlier, whether it is a paper, the implementation or text. In particular:
    10	
    11	- The late positions of the type group outweigh the early text. The type group is the members of the original team who built the type checker and the compiler in the project's last years, 2010 to 2012. Their late positions include the exclusion rule; compiled code specialized to each instantiation of a generic, which they kept; the compiled number tower, which they flattened in 2011; the 2012 write-up on the Return Type Rule (`Papers/Types/journal/`); and the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`).
    12	- The implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text.
    13	
    14	`explorations/coordinator/map/design-intent-sources.md` lists where the designers' intent is written. How a feature is used is the library's practice (`library.md`). `Specification/library/apis/*.tex` is generated from the library, so do not cite it as an independent standard.
    15	
    16	## Changing the text: the revision form
    17	
    18	Record the reason for every change, so that the text and the implementation never disagree where nobody can see it. A change is an edit of the original tree: say so in its commit message. No test can observe a change of prose, so it has no failing test (`tests-writing.md`). A change has four parts:
    19	
    20	1. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build. Do not use `\note`.
    21	
    22	       \revision{<label of the Appendix I entry>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
    23	
    24	   `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines the macro. It prints a labelled box that points to the entry's section.
    25	2. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`. The entry is a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. It gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its effect, the original text quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, and what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need. Each entry names the decision on record that it follows (an entry of POSITIONS, `records.md`), or gives its own reason. Read the existing entries for the form.
    26	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
    27	4. The full reasoning, in a decision record under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. The existing decision records are `explorations/compile-ladder/*/decision-record.md`. Read `rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` for the form.
    28	
    29	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules and soundness claims. Add a callout that says what a calculus predates.
    30	
    31	In your report, quote every sentence of the specification that your change makes false, with its file and line. Such a sentence can be an Appendix I effect, or a note on walk or on the compiled path. Then it can be corrected.
    32	
    33	## When the text and an implementation disagree
    34	
    35	- If the decisions on record settle it, fix the side that they settle.
    36	- If they do not settle it:
    37	  - Leave the text as it is.
    38	  - Write a ledger row that records the departure.
    39	  - Write a gated `XXX` test that asserts the text's answer on the path that departs (`tests-writing.md`).
    40	  - If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the row among the departures in that entry, so that the text claims no more than holds.
    41	
    42	## Citing it
    43	
    44	- In a test, cite by file and section or entry, never by line (`tests-writing.md`). If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
    45	- In an Appendix I entry, cite the unrevised copy by path and line.
    46	- Inside the text, use `\secref{label}`.
    47	
    48	No suite reads `Specification/`, so an edit there needs no gate run of its own.

=== tests-running.md
     1	# Running tests
     2	
     3	## The two suites
     4	
     5	- `ant testFast` runs four tracks in parallel. Each track is a forked JVM with its own caches. It takes about 9 to 11 minutes and runs about 1,800 tests.
     6	  - compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`.
     7	  - library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
     8	  - othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
     9	  - misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
    10	- `ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder, in four shards. It takes about 3 to 4 minutes and runs about 500 tests.
    11	
    12	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
    13	
    14	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
    15	
    16	- Neither suite compiles. Before a suite, run `ant compileAll` on the code that you mean to test.
    17	- Do not run both suites at once: both delete and reuse `ProjectFortress/test-caches`.
    18	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/<track>/TEST-<class>.txt`.
    19	- `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures. "Tests expected to pass are failing!" gives the same verdict, so do not grep for it.
    20	- Both suites set `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` inside `build.xml`, whatever the shell exports, and give each JVM 768 MB. They keep their temporary files in `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
    21	- The shards split one sorted list by index. A file added to `tests/` moves every later test to another shard. So compare only the sum of the four shards. If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
    22	- Start a suite in the background and poll its log (`session.md`). Do not pipe it through `tail`.
    23	
    24	## Outside the gate
    25	
    26	- `ant testSpecData` runs the specification's extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk. It is not in the gate yet. It joins the gate when its five red examples pass: reductions written without their element type.
    27	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
    28	- Warning: both of these targets run `ant compileAll` first, which deletes the tree's caches.
    29	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Do not put a new test in one of them. A defect that fails today gets an `XXX` test in a gated test folder (`tests-writing.md`).
    30	
    31	## One test, or a few
    32	
    33	### Interpreter tests
    34	
    35	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
    36	
    37	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
    38	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
    39	
    40	- It runs `SystemJUTest`, the class that the shards run, with testSystem's JVM settings. It uses an empty private cache, and a directory that holds only the files that you name.
    41	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
    42	- It takes 15 to 25 s, mostly to analyse the library. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
    43	
    44	To see the real diagnostic that the harness hides, run the program directly:
    45	
    46	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress tests/X.fss
    47	
    48	A test can pass at two heaps and die at the third. `bin/fortress` gives its JVM 256 MB if `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set. Your setup sets 4 GB, and the harness uses 768 MB.
    49	
    50	### Compiled tests
    51	
    52	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They read the tree's `default_repository/caches`, so run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
    53	
    54	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is a fixed folder name, not a placeholder: an earlier batch of changes was called N. There is only one copy of the script.

    87	Warning: `ant testCompiler`, `ant testLibrary` and `ant testOtherCompiler` also exist, but each runs `ant compileAll` first, which deletes the tree's caches.
    88	
    89	The harness reads these switches:

    91	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: SystemJUTest's directory.
    92	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`, `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`.

    95	
    96	## When to run a whole suite
    97	
    98	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
    99	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker or of walk, you may run the suite that your edit reaches, whole, once for each code state, after your last edit:
   100	  - for the checker, the compiler and library tracks;
   101	  - for walk, `testSystem`.

     1	# Writing a test
     2	
     3	## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass
     4	
     5	Start every edit of source code in the original tree from a failing test that you add to the test suite:
     6	
     7	1. Write the test. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
     8	2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the base's code through `old-fortress.sh` (`worktrees.md`).
     9	3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.
    10	
    11	The test and the fix can be in one commit. The test needs no commit of its own.
    12	
    13	In your report, quote two to five lines of the failing run and the passing line, each with its command. Do not commit a capture of either run. Do not prove a result with a one-off script: put the check into a test. Assert each value that matters inside the test: an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled test. What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter. Do not add an expected-output file to the interpreter suite.
    14	
    15	An edit of prose that no test can observe, in `Specification/` or `Documentation/`, has no test and no failure to see. Check its text against the tree and the decisions on record instead.
    16	
    17	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
    18	
    19	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
    20	
    21	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
    22	- It passes if it throws no exception, exits 0, and prints neither `fail` nor `FAIL`. So a passing test must not print those words.
    23	- An api that it imports can be in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`.
    24	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
    25	
    26	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in `compiler_tests/` (or `parser_tests/`), `library_tests/` or `other_compiler_tests/`. The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file that names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
    27	
    28	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
    29	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case
    30	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
    31	    <stage>_<stream>_<check>=text
    32	                               stage: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
    33	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
    34	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
    35	
    36	A `run` with no `run_out` check passes if its output contains `pass` or `PASS`. For example:
    37	
    38	    tests=EqualityRung1
    39	    link
    40	    run
    41	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS
    42	
    43	## Expected failures (XXX)
    44	
    45	An `XXX` test asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. If it starts to pass, the suite goes red.
    46	
    47	- `tests/XXXName.fss` is a gated expected failure.
    48	- A refusal at load under walk: put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test passes if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test passes if the program loads and runs clean.
    49	- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file applies to every stage that the file drives. An `XXX` file with `compile` or `link` demands that the compile fail. An unmet `run_out_*` check fails a run test, whatever the prefix. So:
    50	  - For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test.
    51	  - For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over one component. One has a plain name and drives `link`. The other has an `XXX` name and drives `run`, with a key on output that the failing run prints before it dies (`run_out_contains=REACHED`). If the run dies before any output, use `run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED`. Never use `run_out_contains=PASS`.
    52	  - For a code-generator wall, put the `XXX` on the component name in `tests=`, with `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`. A code-generator wall is a `sayWhat` call or another thrown `CompilerError` for a construct that the code generator does not compile yet.
    53	  - The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. To guard a regression that shows as diagnostics, add a plain `<Name>Link.test`.
    54	  - An `XXX` compile test that is pinned by `compile_err_contains`, and whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure". This is red either way.
    55	
    56	Show the first `XXX` test that your change adds working through the harness itself, placed where the gate reads it. A direct compile and run does not show this. Run it twice through the harness:
    57	
    58	1. As it is: the harness must report an expected failure.
    59	2. Changed for one run so that it passes, then restored: the harness must report it red. For example, add the missing declaration to the test program, or set the expected string to what the run prints.
    60	
    61	### Promoting an XXX test
    62	
    63	If a defect has a gated `XXX` test and you fix the defect, the `XXX` test starts to pass and turns the suite red. So:
    64	
    65	1. Before you edit the code, rename the test without the prefix (`git mv`), to a plain name by its topic. For a compiled test, rename the `.test` file and the `XXX` in its `tests=` line or keys as needed.
    66	2. See the plain-named test fail through the harness on the base's code.
    67	3. Make the fix and see the test pass.
    68	
    69	## How a defect is recorded
    70	
    71	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which. The rest of what a report holds is in `records.md`, "What every report holds".
    72	
    73	1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your gated test.
    74	2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer.      1	# The gate
     2	
     3	The gate is the full check of a tree before it lands on `main`. It takes about 25 minutes. Your brief says whether you run it. If your brief does not ask for it, do not run it: run your own tests, as `tests-running.md` says.
     4

    11	
    12	## What it runs
    13	
    14	Run these steps in this order, on a clean build of the tree:
    15	
    16	1. Check `df -h /`. If less than 1 GB is free, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and check again. (Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs, `build-and-caches.md`.) If less than 500 MB is still free, stop and report.
    17	2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`, then `ant compileAll`.
    18	3. Run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). At once, before anything else compiles into the caches, make two copies of `default_repository/caches` for the ladder regression (step 7).
    19	4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`. Both must have zero failures.
    20	5. Write the summary. Compare each suite's count with the last landed summary. If a count fell or a suite is gone, the gate is red.
    21	6. Do the four-thread atomic runs (below).
    22	7. Do the ladder regression (below).
    23	
    24	The times: `ant compileAll` 25 to 60 s, the library order about 110 s, testFast 9 to 11 min, testSystem 3 to 4 min, the atomic runs about 1 min, the ladder about 4 min.
    25	
    26	## What it writes
    27	
    28	- Write the logs under your tree's `tmp/`. Never commit them.

    33	
    34	## The atomic runs
    35	
    36	The suites run at one thread, so they cannot see a lost update or a race in the class loader's first load. These runs compile fourteen programs and run each one three times at four threads, 42 lines. Run them from `ProjectFortress/`, after the library order:
    37	
    38	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
    39	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
    40	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
    41	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
    42	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }

    45	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
